Per-type branching versus a constraint that does not grant an operation; CODE-44's Limits: "A run-time type test that keeps a working path for type arguments without a capability, or that chooses between behaviours that differ per type, is outside this rule's reach".
`if (x) a(); b();` draws both, but CODE-58's finding names statements sharing a line (readability) and CODE-50's names a statement shown inside a body it is not parsed in.

Not a contradiction although CODE-50 calls spacing that matches the language's precedence "truthful": CODE-53's Limits name that case ("Spacing does not stand in for the parentheses ... `x<<8 + y<<16`"). The misleadingly spaced mix is listed as an overlap.
CODE-52 excepts continuation lines ("a continuation line excepted"), which CODE-56 judges.

CODE-55 drops "a line that a wrapping formatter the project context names would rewrite" and "a line pushed over the limit by a pragma or suppression comment"; CODE-60 judges exactly such suppressions.

A present restating comment versus a missing reason comment; CODE-61's Limits put "a missing comment" outside and CODE-63's put "a comment that is present but restates or contradicts its code" outside.

CODE-25's own bad line `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars` draws both, but CODE-25 asks whether the variable is never read (remove it) and CODE-64 whether a reason is stated; CODE-64's Limits: "whether a given suppression is justified at all rather than explained, are outside this rule."
A restating `@param timeout the timeout` is CODE-68's finding on the entry line, while CODE-65 flags the parameter's declaration line; different lines.
Omitted item versus stale item; CODE-67's Limits: "A doc comment that states an item wrongly or has drifted from the code ... are outside the rule."
A value-returning chain without a final else draws CODE-73 (no default) but not CODE-13, which needs "every branch, the final else included"; different questions.
CODE-37 compares similar routines "that are not overloads of one another"; its Caveat leaves overloads to "another rule", API-13.
An argument write in a get-named routine is CODE-02's; DSN-64's Limits: "a routine whose name reads as a query, predicate, accessor or conversion, which is held to its name, are outside the rule."
API-19 asks about expensive or failing work in a getter ("a remote call, a complex computation, work perceivably slower than reading a field"), CODE-02 about a hidden state change.

API-15 asks whether a routine answers "no result with a value of its ordinary result type that means absence by convention"; CODE-16 asks whether a miss's zero or null is used as an entry, and passes a null its routine documents as the absent result.
API-16 targets "a concrete implementation type", CODE-49 the variance of an interface type (`List<Shape>` vs `List<? extends Shape>`).
Count of parameters versus optional inputs passed by position; a six-optional-input constructor draws both but the questions differ.
DSN-19 asks about "an interface or abstract type", "an option, hook or extension point", not a type parameter.
DSN-49 needs "beside a tag field, optional or nullable fields"; CODE-17's shape has boolean flags and no tag.
A stated reason satisfies ERR-17 but not CODE-47, which asks for a checked operation, a type token or the constraint as result type.
TST-22's Limits admit the tolerance comparison CODE-31 asks for: "A value that needs approximate or semantic equality ... can be compared with a comparison adjusted for approximate equality".

CODE-65's good half keeps `read_timeout_ms: u64` with a comment, while DSN-51 asks for a time type; CODE-65's Limits name that case as outside: "the choice of a longer name or a more specific type instead of a comment".
Numeric versus string literals; CODE-26's Limits: "non-numeric literals ... are outside this rule."
CODE-25's Limits: "Routine parameters, fields, imports and unused routines and types are outside the rule" — the territory of CHG-08, CHG-09 and CHG-10.

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-01 Thesis: "A noun phrase that names what a field or property holds, or what a routine returns ..., is singular for one value and plural for a collection, one that ends in a container word (list, array, map, dict, set, collection) counting as plural"
contradictions.sentence_b: CODE-08 Thesis: "It carries no type prefix in the Hungarian manner (strName, szBuf, dwFlags, bEnabled), no word that repeats the declared built-in, primitive or collection type (nameString, usersInt, userSlice, id_to_name_dict)"
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A container word at the end of a name meets the plurality check only; it repeats the declared collection type, so the fix for a singular name on a collection is the plural noun (items), not a container suffix (itemList).

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-03 Limits: "A letter in one of the conventional roles meets the rule" (Thesis roles: "a loop index or counter (i, j, k), a generic iteration value (v), a coordinate (x, y, z), a caught exception (e)", with no bound on scope)
contradictions.sentence_b: CODE-11 Limits: "Conventional short names hold within their small scope: a loop counter or index (`i`, `j`, `k`), a coordinate (`x`, `y`), ...; a conventional name spread across multiple nested scopes is likely too vague again."
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: The conventional-role exemption covers a letter whose uses stay within a small scope; a conventional letter read across several nested scopes or far from its declaration is judged by its scope, which this rule does not weigh.

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-12 Thesis: "A one-letter parameter name on a public signature stays only where the letter is the conventional name for its role: a familiar letter for a common type that stands for no domain value, such as `x` for a generic floating-point operand ..., `p` for a generic pointer, `r` for a stream reader or an incoming request and `w` for a stream writer or a response writer"
contradictions.sentence_b: CODE-03 Thesis: "The conventional roles are a loop index or counter (i, j, k), a generic iteration value (v), a coordinate (x, y, z), a caught exception (e), a file handle used only inside the block that opens it (f), a type parameter (T, E), and, outside a public interface, a letter that matches the notation of a paper or algorithm" — so `public void copy(Reader r, Writer w)` passes CODE-12 and is flagged by CODE-03 (the CODE-03 -> CODE-12 defer does not fire, since CODE-12 does not flag).
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: A familiar letter for a common type that stands for no domain value — r for a reader or a request, w for a writer or a response writer, p for a generic pointer, x for a generic floating-point operand — is a conventional letter in that role.

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-60 Thesis: "Hand layout that the formatter would rewrite is kept only under the formatter's own documented skip directive, placed where the formatter honours it, and only for a region whose formatted output would lose a structure the hand layout shows, such as the rows of a matrix literal." (Validator: "such as rows and columns of values")
contradictions.sentence_b: CODE-57 Thesis: "Where neither the formatter the project runs on the file nor the language's standard formatter emits the alignment itself, an added or changed line carries the language's ordinary spacing between its tokens and no extra spaces that put a token in a column with a token on a consecutive line" — a matrix whose values are padded into columns under `# fmt: off` is CODE-60's good case and CODE-57's finding; CODE-57's Limits name formatter-emitted columns, delimiter-aligned continuations and a project tolerance, not a skip-directive region.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Columns of values padded by hand inside a region the governing formatter's documented skip directive excludes, where the formatted output would lose the rows and columns the layout shows, such as a matrix literal, are outside the rule.

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-59 Thesis: "On a layout point the guide does not require, because it only recommends a form, permits a form without requiring it, or says nothing, the added line takes the form the rest of its file already uses for that point" — in a file that hand-aligns its assignments and a project with no guide, the aligned added line is the compliant one
contradictions.sentence_b: CODE-57 Thesis: "an added or changed line carries the language's ordinary spacing between its tokens and no extra spaces that put a token in a column with a token on a consecutive line"; its only tolerance is "A project tolerance that permits hand alignment", not a file's established practice.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Hand padding that puts tokens into columns is not an established form an added line must follow: where a file aligns by hand and no formatter emits the columns, the added line may take the language's ordinary spacing.

contradictions.sentence_a: CODE-64 Thesis: "An empty body that is an unintentional omission is fixed by implementing it, and one for an operation that is not yet, or never will be, supported throws an error saying so." (fix: "the body implemented or throwing an error that says the operation is unsupported")
contradictions.sentence_b: CHG-37 Thesis: "Each routine that production code reaches is finished when the change merges: it holds no placeholder that fails at run time whenever it is reached and marks functionality still to be written, such as a call or a raised error whose message says the code is not yet implemented." CHG-37's Limits exempt only a member "deliberately left without implementation", not the not-yet case.
contradictions.resolving_limits_sentence: Where production code reaches the routine, an operation that is not yet supported is not settled by a throwing placeholder; the throwing form answers only an operation that will never be supported, its message saying so.

gaps.concept: Deep nesting: a block nested too deeply inside its routine (CC19 "Taming Dangerously Deep Nesting"). The design note computes a `deep_nesting` signal ("the block depth of an added line inside its routine ... depth of 4 or more") but no card's triggers name it; pending entry 69 holds composite complexity scores, not a nesting-depth bound.
gaps.claim: "Many developers consider code difficult to read if blocks are nested beyond a certain depth."; "This rule enforces a maximum depth that blocks can be nested to reduce code complexity."; `"max"` (default `4`)

gaps.concept: Complex boolean expressions: a condition built from many boolean operators, not broken into named parts (CC19 "Boolean Expressions"); CODE-82 covers only comparison with true/false.
gaps.claim: "Restricts the number of boolean operators (&&, ||, &, | and ^) in an expression."; "Rationale: Too many conditions leads to code that is difficult to read"

gaps.concept: Division by a divisor that can be zero (CC12 "Anticipate divide-by-zero errors"); CODE-30's Limits put "division by zero" outside the rule and no other card or pending entry holds it.
gaps.claim: "If the divisor is zero at run time, a run-time panic occurs." (a curl of SonarSource/sonar-java sonar-java-plugin/src/main/resources/org/sonar/l10n/java/rules/java/S3518.html returned no such text, so that rule is not cited)

gaps.concept: Exact decimal quantities (money) held in binary floating point (CC12): CODE-31's Limits defer it ("Whether a quantity that must be exact, such as money, belongs in binary floating point at all ... are judged by their own rules") and CODE-27's Limits put "the choice of a decimal type for decimal quantities" outside, but no card or pending entry holds it.
gaps.source_path: python/cpython Doc/library/decimal.rst (opening list of the decimal module's advantages)
gaps.claim: "The exactness carries over into arithmetic. In decimal floating point, ``0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 - 0.3`` is exactly equal to zero."; "decimal is preferred in accounting applications which have strict ..." (equality invariants)

gaps.concept: A routine named with a vague verb (handle, process, perform, do) that says nothing of its job (CC7 "Good Routine Names"); CODE-04 covers only filler nouns and its Limits put generic names out ("A generic name such as data or callback is outside the rule").

summary: All 82 cards were read; every pattern-bearing card's triggers match its own bad Example, but CODE-36's lone long_routine signal and the CODE-13, CODE-74 and CODE-75 sets are nested in other cards' triggers. The main findings are 28 deferring pairs: 19 inside the domain, chiefly CODE-59 as the catch-all layout card under seven specific layout cards and CODE-50 over three cards that flag the same misleading layout, and 9 across domains (CODE-18 under API-11 and ERR-13, CODE-16 under ERR-16, CODE-63 under ERR-17, CODE-35 under API-10, CODE-07 under DSN-68, CODE-77 under DSN-60, CODE-67 under DSN-64, DSN-25 under CODE-26), plus six contradictions, each resolvable by one Limits sentence. Facets: 23 cards carry the change-shape step `review` with no basis in their Thesis, two applies_to values are too narrow, three mechanical cards need tracing or judgement, CODE-01's major rests only on comprehension cost, and five row concepts (deep nesting, complex boolean expressions, division by zero, decimal money, vague routine verbs) have no card or pending entry.
